column1: A day on Venus is longer than its year
column2: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.
column3: Our idea of a day is only local.

column1: There are more stars than grains of sand on Earth's beaches
column2: Astronomers estimate around 10^22 to 10^24 stars in the observable universe. That likely outnumbers all the sand grains on Earth's beaches.
column3: Scale in space defeats intuition.

column1: Footprints on the Moon could last millions of years
column2: The Moon has no wind or rain to erase them. Unless a meteorite hits, the Apollo astronauts' bootprints will stay for a very long time.
column3: Without weather, history stays put.

column1: Space is not completely silent to instruments
column2: Sound cannot travel through the near-vacuum of space. But spacecraft record radio waves and plasma vibrations that scientists convert into sound.
column3: Translation reveals hidden signals.

column1: Saturn would float in a big enough bath
column2: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. In a hypothetical ocean large enough, it would float.
column3: Giant does not always mean heavy for its size.

column1: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us
column2: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. From the Sun to Earth, that takes around 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
column3: When you look at the sky, you see the past.

column1: The International Space Station orbits every 90 minutes
column2: The ISS travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. Astronauts on board see around 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.
column3: Speed changes even the rhythm of a day.

column1: Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system
column2: Olympus Mons is about 22 kilometres high, more than twice the height of Everest above sea level. Its base is roughly the size of Poland.
column3: Low gravity lets mountains grow huge.

column1: Astronauts grow taller in space
column2: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can gain up to about 3 percent in height. They shrink back after returning to Earth.
column3: Gravity shapes our bodies every day.

column1: A year on Neptune lasts 165 Earth years
column2: Neptune is so far from the Sun that it takes about 165 years to complete one orbit. It completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.
column3: Distance stretches time.

column1: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm
column2: The storm is wider than Earth and has been observed for at least 150 years. It has been shrinking in recent decades.
column3: Some storms outlast centuries.

column1: The Moon is slowly drifting away
column2: Laser measurements show the Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further from Earth each year. That is about as fast as fingernails grow.
column3: Tiny changes add up over billions of years.

column1: You could fit all the planets between Earth and the Moon
column2: The average Earth–Moon distance is about 384,400 kilometres. The diameters of all the other planets add up to slightly less than that.
column3: Space between things is vast.

column1: Pluto is smaller than the Moon
column2: Pluto's diameter is about 2,377 kilometres, while the Moon's is about 3,475. It was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
column3: Categories change as we learn more.

column1: Mercury is not the hottest planet
column2: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury is beaten by Venus. Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping it above 460°C.
column3: Insulation matters more than distance.

column1: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old
column2: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background put the age of the universe at roughly 13.8 billion years. Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
column3: We are newcomers in a very old story.

column1: Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object
column2: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.
column3: A message in a bottle, sent across the stars.

column1: Some planets orbit two suns
column2: Astronomers have found planets orbiting pairs of stars. Kepler-16b, found in 2011, was the first clear example.
column3: Science fiction keeps turning into science.

column1: Neutron stars can spin hundreds of times a second
column2: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space. The fastest known spin over 700 times a second.
column3: Collapse can create extreme spin.

column1: There is a giant cloud of alcohol in space
column2: Sagittarius B2, a gas cloud near the centre of our galaxy, contains large amounts of ethyl alcohol. It is spread too thin to be drinkable.
column3: Chemistry happens everywhere.

column1: The Sun makes up 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass
column2: All the planets, moons and asteroids together are a tiny fraction. Jupiter holds most of what is left.
column3: One giant dominates the family.

column1: Black holes do not suck everything in
column2: From a distance, a black hole's gravity behaves like any object of the same mass. Only very close in, past the event horizon, is escape impossible.
column3: Myths exaggerate the danger.

column1: Mars has blue sunsets
column2: Fine dust in the Martian atmosphere scatters blue light forward around the Sun. Rovers have photographed bluish sunsets.
column3: Different air paints a different sky.

column1: A spoonful of the Sun's core would be scorching
column2: The Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius. Nuclear fusion there turns hydrogen into helium.
column3: Stars are nuclear furnaces.

column1: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
column2: Earth's orbit is slightly oval. It reaches its closest point, perihelion, in early January, during northern winter.
column3: Seasons come from tilt, not distance.
